summary: Describes the structure of control messages historically used with NTP to monitor and control the NTP application on any IP-attached computer, preserved from Appendix B of RFC 1305. These were used before modern management approaches arrived. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Long ago, clocks were checked with a special set of questions about their settings and status. This writes down that old question-and-answer format for the record.

questions: how did ntpq query ntp servers
why is ntp mode 6 not recommended
subtitle: The legacy mode 6 and mode 7 messages used to query and configure NTP servers, documented for reference and not recommended.

tldr.problem: NTP version 4 (RFC 5905) did not carry over the control messages that RFC 1305 had defined, yet tools such as ntpq still relied on them to monitor and configure a running NTP server.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9327 documents the mode 6 control message: a 12-byte header followed by up to 468 bytes of mostly ASCII data, with opcodes for reading and writing variables, setting traps and changing configuration, plus status words and a short description of the mode 7 format.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Historic and says it is not meant to encourage deployment. Its Security Considerations section lists amplification, time-shifting and replay risks, and says use of the legacy mode 6 interface is NOT RECOMMENDED.

today: RFC 9327 has Historic status and was published for the historical record as a reference to the control messages first described in RFC 1305, updated to fit RFC 5905. The text recommends against using the legacy mode 6 interface in new deployments.

sections.title: Why These Messages Exist
sections.content:
RFC 1305 described a set of control messages for the Network Time Protocol for use when no full network management system was available. When NTP version 4 was written up in RFC 5905, those definitions were not carried over. Support for them is not required to conform to RFC 5905.

RFC 9327 records them as a current reference. The mode 6 control messages are used by NTP management programs such as ntpq when a more robust facility such as SNMP is not available. They provide basic control and monitoring of a running NTP server and are not designed for communication between running NTP servers.

The document states that its publication is not meant to encourage development and deployment of these messages. It also describes the mode 7 Remote Facility format, but the commands inside mode 7 messages are implementation specific and not standardized.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a clock with a little service hatch that lets a technician ask "how are you doing?". This document describes how that hatch worked, but does not say to build new ones.

sections.title: The Control Message Format
sections.content:
A control message follows the UDP header. Its first octet carries the Leap Indicator (set to b00), a 3-bit version number and the Mode, which is 6 for control messages. Next come the R (response), E (error) and M (more) bits and a 5-bit opcode, then a 16-bit sequence number, status, Association ID, offset and count. That is three 32-bit words of header.

The data field holds up to 468 bytes and is mostly free-form ASCII so people and simple tools can read it. If authentication is used, the data is zero-padded to a 32-bit boundary and an authenticator follows.

Large responses are split into fragments. Each fragment has the offset of its first octet and a count of its octets, and the M bit is set on all but the last. A request has a distinct nonzero sequence number and R and E set to zero. The reply echoes the sequence number and sets R to one. If the request is invalid, the responder sets both R and E to one and may put a diagnostic in the data.

The Association ID selects what a command is about: zero means the system itself, and a nonzero value means a particular peer association.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a form with boxes for "what do you want", "which clock", "which page of the answer" and "how long is the answer". The reply copies your ticket number so you know which question it answers.

sections.title: Status Words
sections.content:
Every response carries a 16-bit status word in one of several formats. The system status word holds a 2-bit leap indicator, a 6-bit clock source, a 4-bit event counter and a 4-bit event code. The peer status word holds a 5-bit peer status, a 3-bit selection value, and a 4-bit counter and event code. A clock status word reports the state of reference-clock hardware, and an error status word carries an 8-bit error code.

Event counters count repeats of the same code and stop at 15. System event codes include 5 for clock synchronized, 8 for no system peer and 11 for leap second inserted or deleted. Selection values range from 0 for rejected to 6 for system peer and 7 for a pulse-per-second peer.

Error codes in an error response include 1 for authentication failure, 3 for invalid opcode, 4 for unknown Association ID and 7 for administratively prohibited. Values 8 to 255 are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: The status word is a tiny report card: is the clock in sync, where does it get its time, and what was the last thing that went wrong.

sections.title: The Commands
sections.content:
Command data is a comma-separated list of identifier=value items, where identifiers are the names of system or peer variables from RFC 5905. Timestamps are written in seconds and fractions, preferably in hexadecimal, and delay, offset and dispersion are written in milliseconds.

The basic opcodes are Read Status (1), Read Variables (2), Write Variables (3), Read Clock Variables (4) and Write Clock Variables (5). Read Status with Association ID zero lists every association and its status word. Set Trap (6) and Trap Response (7) let a monitor receive asynchronous reports of exception events, using the address and port of the message that set the trap. Unset Trap (31) removes a receiver.

Later commands cover Configure (8), Save Configuration (9), Read MRU list (10), Read ordered list (11) and Request Nonce (12). The nonce is 96 bits long and shows the server that the requester can receive datagrams at its claimed source address, which makes spoofing harder in a similar way to the TCP three-way handshake. Read ordered list requires authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The commands are the things you can ask the clock helper: "tell me your settings", "change this setting", or "ring me if something goes wrong".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that a number of vulnerabilities have been identified. Overwriting variables requires authentication by default, but reading does not, and the document argues that hosts must authenticate all control queries or use an access control list.

The main risks it names are amplification, because some control queries produce a very long response to a short query (the mode 7 monlist command is the example), time-shifting, because an off-path attacker who can read variables such as xmt and rec can spoof server responses, and fast scanning, since mode 6 messages are small UDP packets. Mode 6 and 7 messages are also open to replay, and the nonce gives only limited protection.

Best practice is to configure NTP with the no-query parameter. The RFC states that use of the legacy mode 6 interface is NOT RECOMMENDED and SHOULD NOT be used in new deployments or implementations, and that remote access needs protection such as strict ACLs.
sections.plainLanguage: If anyone can ask the clock helper anything, bad people can use it to shout at others or to trick clocks. So the advice is to keep the hatch locked.

fields.name: LI
fields.desc: Set to b00 for control requests and responses.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: 1 on all fragments except the last.

fields.name: Status
fields.desc: System, peer, clock or error status word.

fields.name: Association ID
fields.desc: Zero for the system, nonzero for a peer.

fields.name: Offset
fields.desc: Offset in octets of the first data octet.

fields.name: Count
fields.desc: Length of the data field in octets.

items.label: Read status
items.desc: Status word, or list of associations when Association ID is zero.

items.label: Read variables
items.desc: System or peer variables and values.

items.label: Write variables
items.desc: Updates variables from a list of assignments.

items.label: Set trap address/port
items.desc: Registers where trap responses are sent.

items.label: Trap response
items.desc: Sent when an exception event occurs.

items.label: Runtime configuration
items.desc: Applies data as if from the configuration file.

items.label: Export configuration
items.desc: Writes the current configuration to a file.

items.label: Remote address stats
items.desc: Recently seen remote addresses and statistics.

items.label: Ordered list
items.desc: List ordered by IP address; requires authentication.

items.label: Client-specific nonce
items.desc: Returns a 96-bit nonce for the requester.

items.label: Unset trap
items.desc: Removes the requester from the trap receivers.
